## Slicing a Rectangle
Do you remember the join and meet from Geometric Algebra? Will be handy for slicing!

- Say your slice goes from point $P$ towards direction $D$ in world space. 

- The slice line can be written using the join product ($\vee$):

$$ \text{Slice Line in World Space} = P \vee D$$

- Put this line into the model space of the object being cut using the sandwich with the motor $M$ that takes you from world to model space (works if no scaling):

$$ \text{Slice Line in Model Space} = M(\text{Slice Line in World Space})M^{-1}$$

## Slicing a Rectangle
A rectangle is made up of four vertices, which makes four edges.

- The slice will make two new shapes out of the rectangle
- Use Math2d's `OrientedDist(vertex, lineModelSpace)` to decide which shape each vertex goes in
- Now we gotta figure out where the slice line cuts any edges
- Make the edge line from $\text{Vertex}_1$ to $\text{Vertex}_2$ using the join ($\vee$)

$$ \text{Edge from 1 to 2} = \text{Vertex}_1 \vee \text{Vertex}_2$$

- Then make a new vertex where the slice line meets the edge using the meet ($\wedge$)

$$ \text{New Vertex} = (\text{Slice Line in Model Space}) \wedge (\text{Edge from 1 to 2})$$

- Add the new vertex to both shapes, and then check the other three edges

## Slicing a Box
Once you wrap your head around Geometric Algebra, going up one dimension is surprisingly similar.

- Imagine a blade in world space with hilt position $H$, tip position $T$. Join them to make a slice line:

$$ \text{Slice Line in World Space} = H \vee T$$

- The blade is sweeping along direction $S$. Join that with the slice line to make a slice plane:

$$ \text{Slice Plane in World Space} = (\text{Slice Line in World Space}) \vee S$$

- We need the slice plane in the model space of the box. If you have a Motor $M$ that takes you from World to Model Space (no scaling please!), you can use the sandwich:

$$ \text{Slice Plane in Model Space} = M(\text{Slice Plane in World Space})M^{-1}$$

## Slicing a Box
A box is made up of six faces, and each one slices like a rectangle.

- The slice will make two new 3D shapes
- Use Math3d's `PMath.distance(vertex, planeModelSpace)` to decide which shape each vertex goes
- To figure out where the slice plane cuts the edges, first choose a face and make an edge line using the join:

$$ \text{Edge from 1 to 2} = \text{Vertex}_1 \vee \text{Vertex}_2$$

- Then the new vertex would be where the slice plane meets the edge line:

$$ \text{New Vertex} = (\text{Slice Plane in Model Space}) \wedge (\text{Edge from 1 to 2})$$

- Add the new vertex to both shapes, and then check the remaining three edges for the face. Then repeat for the other five faces.

- The cut faces of the new shapes can be made out of triangles fanning out from the centre
